how.checksIntro: Every check IAMAI runs, generated from the rules the code runs from.
limitsList: IAMAI approximates how Microsoft evaluates a sign-in; report-only is the truth. Some conditions, like device filters and token state, it cannot reproduce.
Without Entra ID P1 there is no impact analysis; the plan is licence, then security defaults, then Conditional Access.
Sign-in history shows behaviour under today's policy; it cannot see who would register MFA when first prompted.
There is no server: no scheduled re-scans, no alerts, no state shared across devices.
A sign-in session lasts about a day; the plan file never depends on it, so save the plan to keep it.

how.limitsFeedback: Something wrong or unclear? feedback@getiamai.com — I would rather hear about it than not.
how.hostingBody: getiamai.com is a static site: files on GitHub Pages, served through Cloudflare. Your tenant's data is not part of that. The scan calls Microsoft Graph from this browser and the snapshot stays here, so nothing Cloudflare or GitHub serves has ever held it. The source is public and inspectable on GitHub. One thing IAMAI does not control: Cloudflare adds its own page-load beacon to the HTML it serves. So the host measures page loads and network timing for this site. That beacon is not in IAMAI's bundle and cannot be taken out from here, only from the Cloudflare account. It measures the page, not the scan, and carries nothing from your tenant.
how.creditBaseline: The default baseline is Jon Hope's Defense in Depth, published at ConditionalAccess.Tech. IAMAI pins a reviewed version of it and reads it unchanged.
how.creditAnalyzer: CA Policy Analyzer by Jon Hope
how.creditAnalyzerNote: A separate open-source project by the same author, credited here alongside the baseline. IAMAI is a different tool and is not affiliated with it.
how.creditsNote: Microsoft MVP is an award for community contribution. It is not a Microsoft certification of this baseline, and Microsoft does not endorse or support IAMAI.

alerting.title: Alert on Emergency Account Sign-ins
alerting.why: An emergency account should almost never sign in, so any sign-in is a drill or an incident, and both are worth knowing about.
whatToDo: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Monitoring & health → Diagnostic settings → send SignInLogs to a Log Analytics workspace (or the SIEM you already use).
Create an alert rule on that workspace: SigninLogs where UserPrincipalName is one of {list:emergencyAccountUpns}.
Send it to a mailbox or channel somebody reads every day; test it with one sign-in and confirm the alert arrives.
Log Analytics ingestion is billed; a small tenant's sign-in logs cost a few dollars a month.
Defender XDR or your SIEM can take the same rule.
doneWhen: A test sign-in by an emergency account produced an alert somebody saw.

hardening.title: Harden Emergency Access
hardening.why: Minimum emergency access is in place, and this hardening was deferred so the rollout could continue. Until it is fixed, one failure could still cost the way back in.
whatToDo: Scan again once these are fixed: the row closes when they pass.
doneWhen: Every deferred emergency access recommendation passes on a scan.

whatToDo: Renaming changes no evaluation; do it in one sitting.
doneWhen: Every policy name follows {convention}.

whatToDo: Compare {list:overlaps} side by side; keep the one that matches the baseline and set the other to Off, then delete it after a week with no failures.
doneWhen: One policy per control remains.

whatToDo: Sign in with each emergency account from a private browser window, on a device the policies do not trust, and confirm the alert fires.
Record the date in the plan file. Repeat every 90 days.

steps.title: Create or Correct Emergency Access Accounts
steps.why: Emergency access accounts are how you keep access to {tenant} if a change goes wrong.

who.lead: The emergency access accounts, and every policy that must exclude them:
who.policiesNotExcluding: Policies that do not yet exclude the exclusions group: {list:policiesNotExcluding}; fixed in Create or Correct Exclusions Group, never by excluding these accounts directly.
who.operatorNote: Your own account, {operator}, is not one of these and must not be.

decision.label: Emergency access accounts
decision.help: Add every account that exists only for this purpose; two are needed. IAMAI nominated these from names, roles and exclusions; a nomination is not a choice, so no account is emergency access until you choose it here and save.

whatToDo.lead: Choose the emergency access accounts below and save, then clear what is under Fix before continuing.
create: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Users → New user. Name it so the purpose is obvious ({exampleName}).
Sign-in address on the tenant's own onmicrosoft.com domain; cloud-only; no licence; no department, title or manager.
Roles → assign Global Administrator, active and permanent.

Set a passphrase of at least 20 random characters. Store it offline in two places that different people can reach without signing in to this tenant, for example a sealed envelope in a safe and a second copy with the business owner. Never in a mailbox, a chat, or a password manager that needs this tenant to sign in.
Register a hardware security key (FIDO2) for each account and keep it with the passphrase. Not a passkey in Authenticator: that lives on a person's phone. Do not share a key between accounts.

checkFixes.second-account: Create a second account: one account is a single point of failure.
checkFixes.second-account-none: Create two accounts: one is a single point of failure.
checkFixes.permanent-global-admin: {name}: assign Global Administrator permanently and actively; an eligible role has to activate first, and activation is one of the things a bad policy can block.
checkFixes.cloud-only: {name}: this account is synced from on-premises; recreate it as cloud-only.
checkFixes.onmicrosoft-domain: {name}: move the sign-in address to {onmicrosoftDomain}; a custom domain depends on DNS and on any federation.
checkFixes.excluded-everywhere: {name} is inside {list:policies}: add the exclusions group to each policy's Users → Exclude → Groups in Create or Correct Exclusions Group. Do not exclude the account itself.
checkFixes.no-dynamic-group: {name} is a member of the dynamic group {group}, which a policy targets; remove it or change the rule.
checkFixes.mfa-method: {name}: register a hardware security key (FIDO2) and keep it with the passphrase; not a passkey in Authenticator, which lives on a person's phone.
checkFixes.shared-authenticator: {name} shares the Authenticator device {device} with {otherAccount}; move it to its own security key or passkey.
checkFixes.not-a-person: {name} looks like a person's account (it has {attribute}); use a dedicated account instead.
checkFixes.report-only-excluded: The report-only policies {list:policies} do not exclude the exclusions group either; same fix, in Create or Correct Exclusions Group.
checkFixes.managed-policies-excluded: The Microsoft-managed policies {list:policies} do not exclude the exclusions group; Microsoft turns these on itself. Same fix, in Create or Correct Exclusions Group.
checkFixes.phishing-resistant: {name}: register a hardware security key; text and call codes are taken by a swapped SIM.
checkFixes.method-diversity: Both accounts depend on {method} alone; give one of them a different method type.
checkFixes.auth-methods-migration: Finish migrating to the authentication methods policy (the per-user MFA setting can block a recovery sign-in): Entra admin center → Entra ID → Authentication methods → Policies → Manage migration → Migration complete.
checkFixes.no-licence-no-mailbox: {name} holds {licence}; remove it. An emergency account needs no mailbox.
checkFixes.recent-sign-in: {name} signed in {ago}, not a recorded drill: confirm who signed in and why.
checkFixes.display-name: {name}: rename so the purpose is obvious to whoever finds it next, for example {exampleName}.
checkFixes.drill-due: {name}: sign in once to prove the account still works, then record the drill in Cleanup.
checkFixes.credential-storage: Store each passphrase offline in two places that different people can reach without signing in to this tenant.
checkFixes.sign-in-alerting: Alert on every emergency account sign-in (Cleanup: Alert on Emergency Account Sign-ins).

doneWhen: Every check under Fix before continuing passes on the next scan.
Each hardening recommendation passes, or is deferred to Cleanup.

lockedOut.label: If a change locks you out
steps: Sign in with one of the emergency accounts above, in a private browser window.
Entra admin center → Entra ID → Conditional Access → Policies → open the policy that changed today → Enable policy: Report-only (or Off) → Save. It applies within minutes.

If the portal itself is blocked: sign in from a device and network the policies trust (a managed laptop on the office network), or from any device run Connect-MgGraph -Scopes Policy.ReadWrite.ConditionalAccess and then Update-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy -ConditionalAccessPolicyId <id> -State enabledForReportingButNotEnforced.
If no route works, Microsoft support can help; they will ask for the tenant id: {tenantId}.

risks.text: A dynamic group rule re-evaluates on its own, so an account outside a policy today can be inside it tomorrow.
Microsoft-managed policies start in report-only and are turned on by Microsoft, no less than thirty days later.
A mailbox on an emergency account is somewhere to phish and somewhere for mail to sit unread.

steps.title: Use Separate Accounts for Admin Work
steps.why: An admin account that also reads mail and joins Teams meetings is phished like any other mailbox; the admin policies then guard an account that is open all day.

who.lead: {n} people hold a directory role and use that same account for mail or Teams since {from}:

whatToDo.lead: For each person:
steps: Create a second, cloud-only account for the role, named so the purpose is obvious (adm- and their name); no licence, no mailbox.
Move the directory role to it: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Roles and administrators → the role → Add assignment; then remove the role from the everyday account.
Register a passkey or security key on the admin account before its first use; the admin policies require one.
Keep mail, Teams and files on the everyday account; open admin portals with the admin account only.

doneWhen: No account with a directory role has mail or Teams sign-ins in the records.
steps.ifWrong: Put the role back on the everyday account; nothing else changes.

risks.text: An admin who keeps doing admin work from the everyday account never sees the separation; moving the role is what makes it real.

helpDesk: An admin refused by a portal on the everyday account: the role moved; sign in with the admin account.
more.manager: Admin work moves to accounts that do nothing else, so a phished mailbox is not a phished tenant. Without this, every admin inbox is a way in to every setting.

whatToDo.lead: Security defaults are the whole control surface on this licence. Turn them on.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Overview → Properties → Manage security defaults.
Enabled → Save.
Tell everyone they will be asked to register Microsoft Authenticator at their next sign-in, and give anyone who cannot a way to reach the help desk.

doneWhen: Security defaults report Enabled, and everyone who holds a role has registered a method.

whatToDo.lead: Create two emergency accounts and prove they work, before anything else on this list can lock somebody out.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Users → New user, twice, on the tenant’s onmicrosoft.com domain and with no licence.
Give each one Global Administrator, and a long random password stored where two people can reach it without signing in to this tenant.
Sign in with each account once, and write down the date.

doneWhen: Two emergency accounts exist, each has signed in at least once, and their passwords are reachable without a working sign-in to this tenant.

whatToDo.lead: Find what still authenticates the old way, so blocking it later breaks nothing you did not expect.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Monitoring & health → Sign-in logs, and add the Client app column.
Filter the last 30 days to the legacy clients: Exchange ActiveSync, IMAP, POP, SMTP, Other clients.
For every account that appears, find the application behind it and move it to modern authentication, or retire it.

doneWhen: Thirty days of sign-in logs show no successful legacy-client sign-in, or every one left has a named owner and a date it moves.

whatToDo.lead: An app password is a credential that skips MFA. Retire what needs one, then stop new ones being made.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Authentication methods → Policies, and find the accounts that still hold app passwords.
Move each application behind them to modern authentication.
Turn app passwords off once nothing depends on them.

doneWhen: No account holds an app password, and the tenant no longer allows a new one to be created.

whatToDo.lead: Per-user MFA prompts on its own terms and overrides whatever else decides. Move it to the methods policy.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Authentication methods → Policies → Manage migration → Migration in progress.
Under Policies, enable every method people actually use, so nobody loses the one they have.
Entra admin center → Entra ID → Users → Per-user MFA, and set every account to Disabled.
Manage migration → Migration complete.

doneWhen: The tenant reports Migration complete, and no account is left Enabled or Enforced for per-user MFA.

whatToDo.lead: Give each admin a second account that holds the role and nothing else, so a phishing email opens a mailbox and not the tenant.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Users → New user, one per person who holds a directory role, with no mailbox licence.
Assign the role to the new account and remove it from the daily-driver account.
Register a method on each new account, and confirm the person can sign in with it before the old assignment goes.

doneWhen: Every directory role is held by an account with no mailbox, and no daily-driver account holds one.

whatToDo.lead: Global Administrator can undo anything, including the controls on this list. Bring the count down to what the work needs.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Roles & admins → Global Administrator, and list who holds it and why.
For each holder who does not need the whole tenant, assign the least role that does their job instead.
Leave the emergency accounts alone; they are counted here, and they are the way back in.

doneWhen: Between two and four accounts hold Global Administrator, the emergency accounts among them, and everyone else holds a narrower role.

whatToDo.lead: Remove the guests nobody sponsors, so what is left is what any later guest control has to protect.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Users, filter User type to Guest, and add the Creation time and Last sign-in columns.
For each guest, find who invited them and whether the work is still running; delete the ones nobody owns.
Delete the invitations that were never accepted.

doneWhen: Every remaining guest has a sponsor and a reason to be there, and no invitation is left pending.

whatToDo.lead: An account nobody signs into is an account nobody watches. Disable the silent ones.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Users, add the Last sign-in column, and sort by it.
For each account silent for 90 days, confirm with its manager that it is not a shared or seasonal login.
Set Block sign-in on the ones nobody claims, and delete them after 30 days if nothing surfaces.

doneWhen: No enabled account has been silent for 90 days, or each one that has is recorded as deliberate.

whatToDo.lead: Text and call codes are the tier an attacker can intercept without touching the phone. Move people off them before turning them off.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Authentication methods → Policies, and enable Microsoft Authenticator and passkeys for everyone.
Ask the people still on text message or voice call to register Authenticator, and give them a date.
Set Text message and Voice call to disabled once nobody is relying on them.

doneWhen: Text message and voice call are off in the authentication methods policy, and everyone who used them has registered Authenticator or a passkey.

whatToDo.lead: Put the trusted location right: its addresses decide who is never challenged, so every policy that names it inherits whatever is wrong with it.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the trusted location passes on the next scan.

whatToDo.lead: Put the allowed-countries list right: a country missing from it is a person refused at the door, and one wrongly in it is a door left open.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the allowed-countries list passes on the next scan.

whatToDo.lead: Put the pilot group right: it decides who meets a new control first, so who is in it is who absorbs the mistake.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the pilot group passes on the next scan.

whatToDo.lead: Settle the service accounts: an account with no person behind it cannot answer a prompt, so a policy that reaches one stops a job rather than an attacker.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the service accounts passes on the next scan.

whatToDo.lead: Put the authentication strength right: it is the exact list of methods a policy will accept, so anything wrong in it is either a method nobody has or one nobody should be allowed.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the authentication strength passes on the next scan.
